decisions.summary: The legacy tree is always FROZEN; REGEN_FROZEN=1 and PROFILE=1 go with the deleted Python engine they acted on.
decisions.why: The knobs acted only on Python engine files this task deletes (FR-001); nothing in the request asks for frozen legacy sheets to stay regenerable, and FR-002 lets a tool's usage differ so long as it does its job for its callers. A removed debug switch is not a wrong outcome.

decisions.summary: make map MAP=<folder|file|name> and MAP=--all run any pool map, hamlets included, printing CACHED, REGENERATED with reason, or FROZEN; GEN= is refused naming the MAP= form.
decisions.why: make stays the one entry point (FR-005); a usage change is allowed by FR-002, and the refusal points the caller at the new form, so callers still get their job done. Hamlets being drawable widens rather than narrows.

decisions.summary: Engines draw into a staging folder; Mode A reports looked-for-but-missing files as reads; a read changed during a run leaves the map drawn but unpublished so the next run redraws it; both pinned red first.
decisions.why: Fixes two named defects of the old key (a sheet left stale when a looked-for file is created later; a race), which the GM's 2026-11-18 'fix all known bugs in each step' asks for. These are wrong outcomes (a stale map served), not mere differences.

decisions.summary: The six .gen.py, interactive/sheet.py, pipeline/regen.py and pipeline/rollcache.py are deleted unread; bundle_door's is_current asks the cache in process.
decisions.why: FR-001 (every Python file replaced) and FR-003 (replacement passes, then the Python goes; no piece runs both).

decisions.summary: New since the last CLEAR: render_cache.py's own index, which finds maps by .gen.py, would now list nothing, so sync-with-main.sh writes the Rust index (make pool-index, 30 maps) after render-sync under the same lock until T222 deletes render_cache.py and that line.
decisions.why: It fixes a defect this task's deletions caused (an empty index page is a wrong outcome for its readers) in the same task instead of carrying it, as FR-002 ('what a caller reads of it ... it still finds') and the GM's 'fix all known bugs in each step' require. The bridge is temporary, its end named (T222), and T222 lands before T158 and before the next step's port, so nothing is left broken across a step boundary. It narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: New since the last CLEAR: no before-and-after page is published because no drawn sheet changed - the four hand sheets match main's and the two generated sheets differ only by the old render cache's stamp comment (observed 2026-11-19 by cmp and a line diff).
decisions.why: The request attaches the page to the engine slice, not to each task: 'each engine slice publishes a page of every pool sheet before and after' (request.md, 2026-11-17, 'the engine slices worked deliberately'). Whatever page the step owes falls due at the slice's close (T158), and this block does not take it away. Read that way, the block's 'no before-and-after page is owed' means none is owed by this task, and in that reading it narrows nothing. Its limit: the label's comparison covers six sheets, four hand sheets and two generated ones, while the block also says render-sync drew every live map and the pool index lists 30. The bundle does not show that those six are every pool sheet the slice's page must cover. So this decision does NOT stand as proof that no pool sheet moved, and it does NOT excuse the slice's page at T158. A byte comparison offered as evidence of no change is not held as a standard here.

decisions.summary: A warm all-hit run counts pool 1,589 against budget 1,894 and legacy 170 against 170; warm --all 0.1 s, cold 22.6 s.
decisions.why: Holds the derivation's work budget, which is what the GM's 2026-10-30 efficiency rule and the 2026-11-19 plan ask for. Each figure carries a dated method label.

decisions.summary: gencache.py and _census.py stay because main's render_cache.py imports them until T222 deletes all three.
decisions.why: FR-003: Python stays until what reads it is replaced. The deletion is put off to T222 inside the same step, before T158 and before the next step's port, so FR-001's reach is not narrowed.

decisions.summary: New since the last CLEAR: after T227 and T225, then T229 (a guard fix, no port), then T222, both landing before T158 (the step's close) and before the next step's port.
decisions.why: This is the order the GM's 2026-11-18 rule requires: each step's known defects are fixed before the next step's port begins.

decisions.summary: Checks still reading what no longer exists (measure probe's pool changes matching nothing, preflight's roll-census read, land's census variable filter) and whether one failing map should stop render-sync are put on T222's line; the Python cache's old .gencache/<map>/ entries are left on disk.
decisions.why: A check that matches nothing passes everything, which counts as a defect, but it goes to T222 inside this step, before T158 and the next port, which satisfies 'fix all known bugs in each step before moving on'. The stale .gencache entries are a one-time remnant that nothing writes to or reads any more. No map, check or tool gives a wrong outcome because of them, and FR-013 covers what the tooling keeps making, not a past pile, so this is a leftover, not a defect.

decisions.summary: Every map regenerates once on the first run (new cache); a spec edit now counts as drawing code for reviews owed; make verify and the review gate draw hamlets too.
decisions.why: Consequences of the sound read set the GM's rebuild asks for: a spec a map reads is an input of that map. These widen coverage and narrow nothing that was asked.

decisions.summary: The Rust tools build as one cargo workspace (root rust/Cargo.toml naming phases and guard); rust_checks.py runs each member and skips the workspace's own manifest, which builds nothing.
decisions.why: Build layout for the port the GM asked for ('making this a Rust codebase'); the checks still cover every crate (FR-004) through make (FR-005). rust_checks.py staying Python for now is allowed by FR-003 and is itself in FR-001's census, so nothing is carved out.

decisions.summary: serde_json is the one crate added.
decisions.why: A dependency choice inside the port; it narrows nothing the request or spec asks for.

decisions.summary: The guard protocol and its merge of verdicts carried from D1, D2 and contracts/guard-protocol.md.
decisions.why: Implements FR-007 (one process per tool call) and FR-002 (same verdicts); no case of the hooks is excluded.

decisions.summary: The shared state is kept and the facts are asked once.
decisions.why: Carries the measured design fixes over as FR-006 requires; no behavior the GM asked to change is preserved by it.

decisions.summary: The wrapper keeps the last good binary.
decisions.why: A build-failure fallback to an earlier Rust binary, not a return to Python; it does not run a piece twice (FR-003) and does not exempt any piece from the port.

decisions.summary: The settings switch lands with an empty guard list, its own cost recorded as phase 1's floor.
decisions.why: FR-003 keeps the Python guards the ones that run until each replacement passes, so landing the switch with no guards moved is the ordering the spec requires; recording its cost serves FR-010 and SC-001.

decisions.summary: Landed via make land-tooling with no work budget; done is both crates' tests, lint, format, cover and dead clean through make.
decisions.why: Process and exit criteria that enforce FR-004 and FR-005; nothing narrowed.

decisions.summary: T002 builds the one-process hook dispatcher answering Claude Code's protocol with an empty guard list, guards ported later
decisions.why: A first step toward FR-007 (one process per tool call) inside FR-001's hooks-first phase; ports no guard, so FR-002/FR-003 are untouched (no Python replaced, none run twice).

decisions.summary: Done when an event with no guard allows in under a millisecond of its own work and every merge case passes; --self-check answers; coverage full
decisions.why: Acceptance targets that serve SC-001/FR-007 and FR-004's coverage floor; the millisecond is a target the plan sets for the empty dispatcher, not a measured figure, and drops nothing the request or spec asks.

decisions.summary: Every merge case in contracts/guard-protocol.md tested, each test under a tenth of a second
decisions.why: Restates FR-008 and the protocol contract; enforcement of what was asked.

decisions.summary: Runs after T001, lands via make land-tooling with no work budget; red exit records the failure, sets the task down, asks the arbiter
decisions.why: Sequencing and process; the GM's request (make this a Rust codebase) is unaffected, and FR-005 keeps make as the entry point.

decisions.summary: Build the shared state every guard reads (guard log, escapes, session clone and name, GM messages) as one library that reads each fact once and writes it in today's formats.
decisions.why: Serves the request's purpose (Python hooks too inefficient, port to Rust) and FR-007 (guards as one process); 'written as today' is FR-002's same-outputs rule. Nothing the request or spec asks is dropped. Note: the block's gloss of FR-006 as 'asked once, the count pinned' is a paraphrase - FR-006 names the import graph, semantic ids and the fixture; read-once shared state is in the same spirit, not a narrowing.

decisions.summary: Green exit: a guard-log line written by Rust is read back by make guard-log exactly as the shell's is, and each read is counted once per process in a test.
decisions.why: Enforces FR-002 (same outputs) and the read-once design; verification of what was asked, not new scope.

decisions.summary: Red exit: record what failed, set the task down, route a process stop to make arbiter-ask.
decisions.why: Process routing; neither narrows nor extends the request.

decisions.summary: Runs after T002; lands via make land-tooling with no work budget; no researched value or constant moves.
decisions.why: Ordering and landing mechanics inside the hooks phase (FR-001's phase order); no requirement is relaxed.

decisions.summary: Done = the library's tests green and its reads counted.
decisions.why: Does not exempt the library from FR-004 (coverage floor) or FR-008 (test time), which still bind every replacement; the checklist omits restating them rather than carving them out.

decisions.summary: With no good binary ever built, the wrapper lets the call through with a notice and a guard-log line
decisions.why: This is plan D7's own outcome, not new in this block. It is held against FR-002, which asks for the same verdicts on every case the tests and suites hold. Having no binary at all is not one of those cases. The case that matches it today is a guard whose Python cannot start, and m:python-dead-fails-open measures that this already fails open (repo-safety exits 0 on a force push to main, make-only prints nothing, gate exits 127). So no verdict gets weaker than today's. Making it fail closed would be new behavior the GM did not ask for. The earlier BLOCKED version justified this from FR-005's make-only clause. The block now cites the requirement that actually governs verdicts.

decisions.summary: A failed build (does not compile, or compiles and fails l7r-guard --self-check) runs the last good binary; a stale build is rebuilt
decisions.why: This repeats D7 word for word, and the self-check is D7's own definition of a good build. Today a broken Python guard crashes and fails open, so keeping the previous guards running gives a verdict no weaker than today's. The request asks for a port and nothing here cuts what it covers.

decisions.summary: T004 replaces no guard; T005 adds the wrapper to the settings with an empty guard list; each guard task moves one decider in and removes that guard's shell script and settings entry in the same landing
decisions.why: This is how the plan carries out FR-003: the Python stays the one that runs until its replacement passes, and no piece runs in both. Separate processes for the guards still being moved are a temporary state. FR-007's one process is where the work ends up, and this order does not give it up.

decisions.summary: FR-005's clause that the make-only guard must cover the replacements' binaries is left to T028, not this task
decisions.why: This assigns the requirement to another task and narrows nothing. The clause is about the make-only guard's coverage, not about the wrapper. FR-005 still applies to the feature in full, and the block names the task that carries it.

decisions.summary: Lands through make land-tooling with no work budget and nothing rolled; no researched value or constant moves
decisions.why: This is process and tooling scope only. Nothing the GM asked for is changed.

decisions.summary: Every session's settings call the one dispatcher once per event, beside the Python guards it does not yet hold.
decisions.why: FR-001 ports the hooks first and FR-003 requires each unported guard's Python to stay the one that runs while no guard runs twice; FR-007's single process is the end state reached as pieces move in. A coexistence period is what FR-003 itself describes, not a carve-out from the GM's request to make this a Rust codebase.

decisions.summary: After T004; landed alone with make land-tooling.
decisions.why: Sequencing and landing route only; the spec leaves both open and neither narrows what is ported.

decisions.summary: Green: settings call it for every event, make hooks-test green, its floor timed. Red: failure recorded, task set down, process stop to make arbiter-ask.
decisions.why: The green exit enforces FR-002/FR-003 (hooks-test) and FR-010 (timed); the red exit stops rather than relaxing any requirement.

decisions.summary: No work budget, nothing rolled, for a tooling landing.
decisions.why: Process bookkeeping; it changes nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: Re-run m:hooks-bash's command with the dispatcher in place and record the floor.
decisions.why: Serves FR-010 and SC-001's measurement against m:hooks-bash; it does not claim SC-001 met or move its target.

decisions.id: T005-6 no constant or room question
decisions.summary: No researched value moves; no constant moved; not a room question.
decisions.why: Statements that the task touches only Claude Code tool-call guards, consistent with FR-009's scope and the request.

decisions.summary: Guard by guard with shell and settings entry removed in the registering commit (D3/FR-003); suite as verdict replay with its inline Python replaced in the same task (D4); order by measured cost first (R2); the two XIV fixes on make-only-hooks and guard-file-hooks (FR-002's exception).
decisions.why: Each is settled by the accepted spec (D3, D4, FR-002's named exception, FR-003) and none is T006's own: the XIV fixes belong to two other guards' tasks, so T006 changes no expected verdict. Putting pair-hooks first agrees with m:hooks-bash, which names it the slowest guard.

decisions.summary: The Rust decider keeps consulting the eight phase-3 Python tools (checkpoint.py, plan_gate.py, review_prereq.py, review_owed.py, gate-stamp.py, make engine-key, hm_arbiter.py, hm_dropped.py) by path on its two rare branches and at Stop, until each tool's own port answers in-process.
decisions.why: FR-001 fixes the phase order (hooks first, tooling in phase 3) and FR-003 requires a piece's Python to stay the one that runs until its replacement passes, so a hook ported in phase 1 has to call the tooling that is still Python. FR-007 asks for one guard process per tool call, not one per guard. It does not forbid the guard calling external tools, and the plain Bash path that SC-001/m:hooks-bash measures reaches none of them. This is temporary sequencing the spec requires, not a carve-out.

decisions.summary: The engine key (a find over l7r/ and pool/, plus make engine-key when the cache is stale) is computed only on the two branches that read it, not on every call.
decisions.why: Removing work that changes no verdict serves the request's purpose (the GM: the Python code is too inefficient), and FR-002's suite replay gates it. Two notes that are not rulings: (1) the citation is stretched, because FR-006 names three specific fixes and the plan's paraphrase 'a fact computed once, and only where it is used' is broader than the text; (2) today every call has a side effect, refreshing the cached key, and the claim that 'no other branch reads it' is shown only by the suite. If anything outside pair-hooks reads that cache and relies on the per-call refresh, FR-002's 'outputs' would cover it. Whether anything does was not measured in this bundle.

decisions.summary: The guard's inline Python state handling (pairing state, review rounds, dispatch record, bypass log, read_field) becomes Rust over the same files and formats.
decisions.why: This is the port FR-001 asks for, and keeping the same files and formats is what FR-002's same-outputs rule requires.

decisions.summary: The suite's "$HOOK" pretool|stop runs l7r-guard --only pair-hooks PreToolUse|Stop through a shared shim tests/hooks/guard-shim.sh, with the suite's cases unchanged.
decisions.why: This is D4 as written: the suite points at l7r-guard --only <guard> and its cases are unchanged. The shim only maps the suite's existing argument form onto the binary's.

decisions.summary: Green: the suite passes against the Rust guard, plus rust-test, cover and hooks-test. Red: record the failure and stop to make arbiter-ask. Landed by make land-tooling with no work budget.
decisions.why: The exits restate FR-002/FR-003/FR-004's gates, and the landing route is process that narrows nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: hm_make.py's targets, combine and classify-through-bare-pytest move to rust/guard/src/shared/make.rs with gate-hooks, patterns verbatim; the rest of hm_make.py moves with make-only-hooks (T028) and guard-file-hooks (T029).
decisions.why: Partitions a shared library across the guards that read it; every part is still ported (FR-001, the request's 'all be ported to Rust'), verbatim patterns keep FR-002's same verdicts, and the suite replay (D4) checks the result. Nothing is left in Python that the request or spec would have ported.

decisions.summary: The decider reads tool_input.command as JSON instead of the shell's greedy sed, so a ' -k ' in the description field no longer arms the subset flag; a suite case is added, the fix named in the commit and the phase's record.
decisions.why: Applies the one exception the accepted FR-002 already states - a guard refusing correct work (a later make done refused on a falsely armed subset flag) is fixed in its port under constitution XIV - with that exception's conditions met: the case lands in the same commit and the change is named in the commit and the phase's record. It narrows nothing the GM asked for; the request is to make the codebase Rust, not to preserve a misparse.

decisions.summary: gate-hooks.sh's status mode is ported: l7r-guard --only gate-hooks status prints the same subset_pending= line, reached through the shim's status mode.
decisions.why: Preserves an existing output as FR-002 requires (same verdicts and outputs); it reverses the dropping the earlier preflight ruled NOT LEGITIMATE.

decisions.summary: After T005, independent of the other guards; green exit is the suite against l7r-guard --only gate-hooks plus rust-test, cover and hooks-test; the shell and its settings entry go in the commit that registers the decider.
decisions.why: Restates D3 (guard by guard, never both, FR-003) and D4 (the suite is the replay), and FR-004's coverage floor; no new scope.

decisions.summary: The sanitized command and the last full gate are read in-process; gatecost.py (asked only on a streak's first expensive measurement, for its reminder's median) stays the measure tool's, asked by path, until phase 3 ports it.
decisions.why: FR-001 orders the port in four phases and FR-003 keeps a piece's Python the one that runs until its replacement passes; gatecost.py belongs to a later phase, so calling it where the shell did is what those require, not a carve-out from them. It is not a guard, so FR-007's one process per tool call is not touched. Nothing the guard decides is left out of the port.

decisions.summary: The shell's greedy read (from the payload's last "command" key to its last quote) is kept for the git commit reset only, reproduced over the input in its own key order.
decisions.why: FR-002 requires the same verdicts as the shell on every suite case, and its only exception (XIV) is for a guard that refuses correct work. A later field naming git commit RESETS the streak, which makes the guard more permissive, so it refuses nothing correct, and the exception does not reach it. Keeping the shell's behavior is FR-002 applied as written. Reproducing the span over the re-serialized input rather than the raw bytes is a design choice; FR-002 judges it on the suite's cases, which the exits require to pass.

decisions.summary: status is ported, printing the same measurements_since_reset=N budget=B line.
decisions.why: FR-002: same outputs as the piece replaced.

decisions.summary: The shell guard and its settings entry are removed in the commit that registers the Rust decider, after test-measure-hooks.sh passes against l7r-guard --only measure-hooks.
decisions.why: Plan D3/D4 and FR-003 (never both), stated as accepted.

decisions.summary: hm_shape.py's wait/sleep/watch/self-matching/ceiling/periodic-report functions move to rust/guard/src/shared/wait.rs with each pattern verbatim; the rest of hm_shape.py (executing_backticks) moves with the guard that reads it
decisions.why: FR-001 replaces every tracked Python file and D3 moves guards one by one; porting the library the guard reads, patterns verbatim, is how FR-002's same-verdicts requirement is met. Nothing is left in Python or dropped - the remainder is assigned to its own guard's port.

decisions.summary: the periodic-report refusal's cron minute stays the local minute, read via `date +%M` only on the backgrounded-periodic-report branch
decisions.why: Keeps the Python's verdict and output (time.localtime().tm_min) exactly, which is what FR-002 requires; the earlier UTC alternative was the deviation and is already rejected. A child process on one rare branch is a mechanism choice, not a second guard process (FR-007 is about one process per tool call for the guards), and it changes nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: self_matching compiles the command's pgrep -f pattern with fancy-regex instead of Python re, skips a pattern it cannot compile as the Python skipped one re could not, and rests dialect-divergence detection on the suite replay
decisions.why: FR-002 scopes equivalence to every case the tests and suites hold, and D4 makes the suite the replay; the decision meets that bound, preserves the skip-on-uncompilable behavior, and states plainly that divergence outside the suite is not covered - which is the spec's own bound, not a carve-out from it. A Rust port cannot use Python's re, so a different engine is inherent to the request.

decisions.summary: The verdict library scripts/hooks/lib/hm_tree.py (judge, explain, log context) is ported whole, each pattern verbatim, to rust/guard/src/shared/tree.rs, shared with gm-tree-hooks, which moves to it in its own task.
decisions.why: FR-001 replaces every Python file and FR-002 asks for the same verdicts; porting the library the verdict comes from, verbatim, is how the guard is ported. Done-measured deletes only main-tree-hooks.sh and its settings entry, so hm_tree.py stays for gm-tree-hooks until that guard's own replacement passes (FR-003, D3).

decisions.summary: The session's clone comes from T003's session facts through the same resolver ported (claim map, last /rename, sessions json), not from spawning clone-sync-hooks.sh resolve.
decisions.why: The same resolution with the same inputs, run in the one guard process FR-007 requires; FR-002's suite replay (D4) checks the verdicts.

decisions.summary: The mirror root comes from walking up to the nearest .git (T006's find_root) and cutting at /.clones/, not from git rev-parse --show-toplevel.
decisions.why: A mechanism change stated to give the same answer, which the suite replay must confirm before the switch (FR-002, D4). It narrows nothing that was asked.

decisions.summary: The refusal and the rewrite's context name rust/guard/src/guards/main_tree_hooks.rs instead of scripts/hooks/main-tree-hooks.sh, which this task deletes; no verdict changes.
decisions.why: This is an exception to FR-002's 'same outputs', and the only exception FR-002 names is the XIV fix, so it is judged as a carve-out. Applied literally, the rule would make the guard send a refused session to a file this same commit deletes. That defeats what the message is for, which is telling the reader where the rule lives. It does not reach what FR-002 is for, proving the port changes no decision, because only the self-referencing path changes and every verdict and all other text stay as they are. The precedent is T006. If a suite case asserts the path, its expected text changes in the same commit and the commit must name that change.

decisions.summary: The hook half of scripts/measure/event_log.py (line, verdict reading, categories, log path, append) moves into the Rust decider with patterns, fields and order verbatim; the from-transcript command stays Python until phase 3 ports the measure tools.
decisions.why: The request is to make the codebase Rust; FR-001 orders the port in phases with the hooks first. The code that runs on every hook event is the hook's, and porting it with the guard is the hooks phase doing its job. The part that is a command, not a hook, goes in the later measure-tools phase, which FR-001's phase order already provides; nothing is excluded from the port. Keeping the line's fields and order the same is what FR-002 requires so that feature-report reads it unchanged.

decisions.summary: On an Edit, the reversal test (hm_arbiter.reversal) runs in-process in Rust; recording the trip is handed to hm_arbiter.py by path, and only when a reversal is found, until the arbiter is ported.
decisions.why: The arbiter is its own piece in FR-001's phase order, and this block does not port it. Calling it by path, and only on the rare reversal, keeps Python off the common path, which is the hook start-up cost the GM's request was about, and it lasts only until the arbiter's own port, so no Python is kept for good. FR-003 is per piece: the guard's verdict comes from Rust alone, so no piece runs both. The block follows T006 (a).

decisions.summary: The log line's ev is taken from the payload's hook_event_name, as the Python did; l7r-guard --only with no event name reads it from the payload, so the suite's "$HOOK" replays unchanged.
decisions.why: This keeps the Python's behavior (FR-002) and lets the guard's existing suite replay against the Rust guard without edits (D4). It is an interface detail that serves the spec and narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: The edit digest stays SHA-1's first 12 hex digits, written as a small SHA-1 in shared beside T006's SHA-256 rather than taken from a crate.
decisions.why: Keeping the digest format is FR-002 (same outputs). Writing the hash in shared rather than using a crate is a design choice, not a fidelity question, and it narrows nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: The tools the guard asks (git, sync-with-main.sh, own-make.sh, gate_lock.py, clone_local_settings.py, solo.py, usage_log.py, layout_carry.sh) stay theirs and are asked by path until their own ports.
decisions.why: The request ports all the Python and the spec phases it (FR-001); FR-003 requires the Python to remain the one that runs until its replacement passes. Each tool is named as ending at its own port, so this is order, not an exclusion.

decisions.summary: The session facts the guard's inline Python read (input fields, canonical clone, whether another claimant is live) are read in-process from T003's facts and /proc; the notice's make targets use shared::make::targets.
decisions.why: This is the port itself, what the request asks for; the block binds it to the same answers, which is FR-002.

decisions.summary: The script stays as its resolve mode only, code unchanged and outside l7r-guard, until T051 deletes its callers; prompt and pretool leave in this task.
decisions.why: Sequencing, not a carve-out: (1) the kept code has a named remover, T051, so nothing is excluded from the port the request asks for and FR-001 phases; (2) the guard runs on one path, since resolve is not a guard mode and both guard modes and both settings entries go in the commit that registers the decider (item 9, D3), so FR-003 is met; (3) FR-002 is untouched, the resolve code being unchanged. The not-through-l7r-guard reasoning (recursion, cargo build) is mechanism and decides nothing here either way. Two points for the record: step 1 says 'its shell gone' while (c) keeps the script, and item 9 is the operative statement; and (b) ports the canonical-clone lookup while (c) keeps the shell's canonical_clone for the other guards, so two implementations are live until T051. That is not FR-003's 'both', each call taking one path, but T051 owes the deletion of the shell's version as well as of its callers.

decisions.summary: The prompt mode's lines are the decider's plain-stdout answer, byte for byte, so the suite's prompt cases pass unedited.
decisions.why: Directly FR-002: same outputs, suite expectations unedited.

decisions.summary: Every mode (stop, prompt, timer, stagger) moves to Rust; the detached wait and printed stagger become the binary's --idle-tests entry, started by setsid nohup as the shell was; the GM's disable of 2026-09-06 carries over as one constant, arming off.
decisions.why: Porting every mode is what the GM's 'making this a Rust codebase' and D3 ask, and leaves no shell behind. Keeping arming off is FR-002 (same verdicts), not a carve-out. FR-007's one process concerns the guards deciding a tool call, not a background wait started the way the shell started it.

decisions.summary: git, setsid, nohup, kill, pgrep and the run itself stay external tools asked by path; the lock is the flock tool on the lock file's descriptor.
decisions.why: These are system tools, not Python or shell in the repository, so FR-001 is untouched and nothing the GM asked for is reduced. The stated semantics (a lock owned by the open file the timer holds, as fd 9 was) keep FR-002. The choice of flock tool over a library call is design, which this mode does not grade.

decisions.summary: The small tools and the Python fragments go in-process (field, state_of, JSON, cksum with the same CRC values, ls -t, clone top); the JSON's keys and values are the same, its key order and indentation are not held.

Placed in scripts/gates/ it is a tracked .py that FR-001's first census returns at every phase end, its removal cannot be skipped (SC-005), and it is moved code rather than new behavior, its life bound to the two files it calls. UNSETTLED BY THE BUNDLE, FOR THE IMPLEMENTER UNDER FR-002: (c) reaches the ask only once a call is not blocked, so the block verdict in (b) runs on the undecoded URL, and the plan does not say whether the Python decoded before the block check or before the heredoc rule; likewise a failed ask leaves archived with no decoded key. decisions.summary: The crash warning goes: the shell told the session when its Python decision could not run; a compiled decision has no import to fail, and a guard that does not run is the wrapper's own notice (T004).

Its purpose, the session being told its guard did not decide, passes to the wrapper's notice (T004) rather than being dropped. decisions.summary: The closed form admits any NAME=value of a plain value before the storing command, PATH included, and states that then no command in the call can run what was stored.
decisions.why: The sentence is false for this member of the form. Run 2026-11-08, bash 5.3.9, with a directory holding a symlink named cat to python3: both a PATH=<dir> prefix on the storing cat and a PATH=<dir> line before it, one call, quoted delimiter, nothing after the terminator, ran the body as Python (a marker file appeared); the real cat as control ran nothing. That is the form the same decision keeps refused, a body handed to an interpreter, and the verdict would change to pass, past the 'one form alone' it promises and past FR-002's exception, which reaches only correct work refused. The setup is one earlier call, and the logged case needs none of it. Fix: no assignment in the call may name PATH or a dynamic-loader variable (LD_*), and a refused case in test-make-only-hooks.sh pins it. Not reopened: the forms already refused; and the store-then-run-in-a-later-call route, which the sentence's 'in the call' leaves out.

The gate reads the state and writes nothing, so one implementation still writes checks-open.json. It is not two implementations of one decision under FR-003: the deciding stays in the Python alone.

decisions.summary: A Bash call that names apply-edits or runs make done by hm_checks' own pattern starts the shell guard.

decisions.summary: While a plan review holds text, EVERY Bash call starts the shell guard and so Python, including an unrelated ls.
decisions.why: This is a real carve-out from 'never on a plain Bash call' and is ruled on its own. Applying the rule literally defeats the purpose: any command can rewrite held text, so no narrower test on the command exists, skipping Python would drop the hold's verdicts against FR-002, and the deciding cannot move to Rust before phase 3 because the settled ruling ports it in one cut. It is confined to the span of a plan review's hold, the 'rare branch' FR-001 names, and ends in phase 3.

decisions.summary: The gate treats Write as it treats Edit, though the goal and FR-001 say plain Edit.

decisions.summary: With no repository there is no state and so no hold, as state_path returning None gives.
decisions.why: Round 1's NOT LEGITIMATE fallback is gone; the case now matches the Python it fronts.

FR-001's phase-3 clause keeps this guard's Python until phase 3 and bars it only on a plain call, so one process on a concerning call is impossible before that cut. decisions.id: item-1/item-6/(d) the goal read as a plain Bash call
decisions.summary: SC-001 ('the guards before a Bash call') is restated as 'a plain Bash call', and the green exit is m:t054-plain-bash under 17.5 ms, while (d) concedes a command with quotes or git still compiles what it needs and the entry records it at quoted_git_ms 29.43-29.73 against target_ms 17.5.
decisions.why: The word 'plain' is not in SC-001; the plan inserted it. The pointer m:hooks-bash in SC-001 supplies the baseline (175 ms, so 17.5), not the scope of calls: that the baseline was sampled on an ls does not make ls the only call the criterion speaks of, and reading it so is completing the thought. Item (d) discloses the gap honestly, but disclosure is not a ruling. Against the tests: not physically impossible (the block does not argue 29 to 17.5 cannot be done); not implied by the GM's words (request.md says nothing about commands that match no pattern; it says hook startup time matters and the Python is too inefficient); the literal reading does not defeat the purpose, it IS the purpose, whereas fast exits that fire only on commands no rule could match meet the number on the instrument's own sample and leave any call with a quote or a git over it. How much of real Bash traffic is plain is unmeasured. CLEAR would need either: item 1 drops 'plain' and item 6 requires both recorded commands under 17.5 ms; or the block names this as an exception to SC-001 and takes it to make arbiter-ask rather than ticking on the plain figure.

decisions.id: (b) fast exits only where the rules cannot fire
decisions.summary: Per-guard early exits, each with its stated reason, after the guard's escape handling; suites and case tables unchanged at the exit.
decisions.why: A means toward SC-001 under FR-002, which item 6 enforces. Whether each 'cannot fire' claim holds is implementation, caught by the suites. The fault lies in treating these exits as enough for SC-001, ruled above, not in making them.

decisions.summary: The two hashes stay equal to the Python's over ast.dump. The dumps are kept by blob under <git dir>/semantic-dumps/; codeid.py --semantic is asked once a run only for the blobs it lacks, so an unchanged tree starts no Python; a form unused for a week is dropped.
decisions.why: This answers the earlier BLOCKED verdict: the block no longer asks about every file on every run, and now matches FR-001's 'one process a run with all the cache's misses in it' and FR-006's kept-cache fix. Keeping the dump rather than the id is what FR-006's fix needs here, since the hash input is the concatenated dumps and no per-file id can rebuild it; FR-001's 'one Python library' concerns the Python callers of later phases and is not contradicted by a Rust-side store. Equal hashes are FR-002's same outputs. Python staying in the path is FR-001's own ruled placement of codeid.py in phase 4, whose failure-fails-the-gate clause this block does not relax. Dropping a form unused for a week is housekeeping of the store this decision creates and narrows nothing asked: a dropped form is only a later miss.

decisions.summary: runlog.py moves to T064 and scripts_readers/tooling_modules to T071, because every caller of each is in that task.

Porting with the last caller avoids a client and is FR-003's one cut, the same placement rule FR-001 applies to shared libraries. The bundle does not show which phase T071 stands in; the ruling rests on the block's statement that every caller is in that task, so it moves no piece past its callers.

decisions.summary: The reach branch, import_graph, _top_names, reached_from_kept and seeded are dropped rather than ported, and three test cases are retired with them.
decisions.why: Code not ported is a narrowing of 'all be ported', presumed wrong, and judged separately from the accepted spec. It is legitimate on the request's own terms: the GM asked that this become a Rust codebase instead of a Python one because the Python is inefficient, and the outcome here is less Python and no surviving behavior lost. The block names the search space that shows no caller (git grep over the code, and specs/448's *.py checked for imports), and with the entries' only source gone the branch has no input to decide on. Taken one at a time: the three helpers exist only for the reach branch; seeded has no importer; of the three retired cases, two exercise the reach branch and one exercises seeded, and every other case of the three test files replays. FR-002 carries the same retirement as a ruled case, so no verdict a live input can reach changes without that ruling covering it.

decisions.summary: load refuses an entry naming no stages, with a test.
decisions.why: Stated verbatim in FR-002's ruled case (ask:449-T72-coverage-exempt): 'load refuses one instead'. A refusal exactly as wide as the accepted spec's, adding no reach of its own.

decisions.why: FR-001 sends each tests/ file with the piece it tests, and these test Makefile recipes. Staying across the recipe switch means they run through make against the Rust-backed recipes, which is FR-002's comparison on those six cases.

decisions.summary: test_the_word_list_is_the_hook_s_own is not replayed because the check and the guard include_str! the one file.
decisions.why: Two readers of one compiled-in file cannot differ, so the case's purpose, one list, cannot be violated and the case has nothing to observe. Adjudicated separately from the moved-table case: different reason, same outcome.

decisions.why: FR-001 places hm_house.py in phase 3 and each test goes with its piece.

decisions.summary: test_the_file_cap_is_found_a_reader is not carried literally; what it guarded is replayed by the_detector_finds_a_real_reader_on_the_real_tree, naming the surviving reader check-function-cap.py and going red if the detector goes blind, and by a planted reader of each kind.

Round 4's open finding, cured as that round asked: the sentence that leaned on make rust-tooling is gone and a named real-tree test stands in it. The literal subject, the Python reader the port removes, cannot survive its own port; the purpose, a detector that sees a real reader on the real tree, is now held by a test that fails if it goes blind. check-function-cap.py is itself deleted late under FR-001, at which point the test goes red loudly, which is the safe direction. FR-008 allows a tool one end-to-end test against the real command, which is the room a real-tree test takes; the plan does not state this test's time, and that is an implementation check rather than a fidelity one.

decisions.summary: fragment_move.py's self-test moves to tests/tooling/test_fragment_move.py.
decisions.why: A relocation that loses no case; each tests/ file goes with its piece under FR-001.

decisions.why: Those cases compare a content cache's answers with and without it; the compiled check has no cache, so the comparison cannot be made. FR-006 names three design fixes and this cache is none of them, and the measured timing shows nothing is lost by omitting it. Resolved in rounds 1-3 and unchanged.

No case is dropped: each still runs against the code that gives the verdict.

Impossibility holds: the case compares two definitions and after the deletion only one exists to compare. Purpose holds: the case exists so that a figure cannot be defined two ways, and review_prereq.py reading the pattern from the Rust verb instead of holding its own is that outcome by construction. It is one case, not a class, and the block names it and its replacement.

decisions.why: FR-002's ruled case ask:449-T066-json-message settles this, and the block states all four of its invariants and names the same instance. The request asks for no byte-identical library text.

Twelve real-cargo tests of l7r-gate rust exceed one, the block neither names FR-008 nor measures the cases against its limit, and nothing makes the rule impossible: the block itself says the World seam's Rust tests exist. FR-002 requires the cases be held, not that each run real cargo. To clear: one end-to-end real-cargo test per tool and the rest over the World seam, or a recorded ruling on FR-008, or, if each subcommand is a tool under FR-008, the block saying so with the count per subcommand.

decisions.id: XDIST PROBE: the T065 clause's last limb
decisions.summary: the probe holds the clause on a plain Bash call, a plain Edit, Makefile parse time and an already-verified make done, but still runs on every other make done, including one picking no Python test, until T071 and phase 4

The make-done limb cannot be held inside the ruled form: the ruling fixes a probe that is itself a Python start on the pytest line, and that line runs on every make done that passes already-verified, so while the line runs the probe runs. The exception is the physically-impossible case, not an awkward one, and it does not gut the clause's purpose, since the same recipe starts python3 -m l7r.diagram.ci incremental and pytest on that make done regardless. It ends where the block says, at T071 and phase 4. The premise that done always reaches test-full is the block's one-shot reading of the Makefile dated 2026-11-09; the bundle bars re-reading the repository, so it was weighed as labeled and not re-measured.

The earlier block kept the bar whole by calling the list's 'Python-file size bar' a mislabel, which completed the GM's thought against what was approved. This block deletes the part the approved list named. The .rs bar and the directory count are not checks on the Python, so keeping them narrows nothing the GM asked about.

Item 1's goal sentence reads more broadly than this and is loosely worded; the decision is the operative text.

The shares change only because FR-001b removed the planner the ruling named; pytest 4 s, preflight 5 s and seeds 8 s cover the 6.9 s gap. The arbiter's quoted ruling is not in the bundle beyond FR-001/FR-001b's references to it, and m: figures were taken as labeled, not re-run, because the MANIFEST forbids reading the repository.

decisions.summary: A make done is judged at the existing 5 s incremental floor instead of the 40 s floor of the pinned ratchet baseline; neither setting's value moves.

SC-002 requires under 15.1 s, which is below a 40 s floor, so keeping that floor would refuse every run that meets SC-002. Item 10 now says this openly in place of the earlier 'None moved'. FR-002 is port equivalence and FR-006 appears only as a first line; neither visibly holds this floor, which the bundle cannot settle further. Noted for the record: the reach is every make done, including one that reuses no crate's checks, where the stated reason does not apply; no clause of the request or cited requirement speaks to that case.

decisions.summary: The verdicts are held by a differential of each command through Python and binary on the real repository and two scratch clones (249 comparisons, 0 differences, one-shot, observed 2026-11-10); argparse usage text and a Python traceback's text are not compared, citing ask:449-usage-text.

The exclusion stays inside that ruling's seam: only stderr argparse generates and an uncaught traceback's text are unbound; exit status and stdout stay held and are among what was compared; a parser.error message, a hand-written usage line or refusal, usage text read by a caller and --help held by a kept suite case stay bound, and the block claims none of those excluded. The figure carries a date and method as a one-shot label; it was not re-run because the MANIFEST forbids the repository. The doubled sentence is a drafting wart, not a fidelity finding.

decisions.why: FR-001 places all three in phase 3, and ask:449-T81-slices has T81 file as separately landable tasks. That ruling's text does not name these three leaves, so their being first is the plan's own choice, inside what was asked. ask:449-T80-order's 'by path until T81 lands' now ends at the task holding reserve-prefix, which ask:449-T81-slices already ties to reserve-prefix landing.

decisions.summary: hm_record.py is ported alone; its Python callers (review_owed, entry_owed, apply_edits, claims_reply, check_bundle) stay Python and reach the port through scripts/record_door.py.
decisions.why: FR-001 (ask:449-hm-checks-route) names hm_record.py and the guards check-bundle, checks and record-edit as 'ported in one cut with their Python callers so that one implementation ever writes checks-open.json and the arbiter files'. The block ports it without those callers, does not name that clause, and cites only ask:449-T81-slices, whose text never names hm_record and is compatible with one separately landable task holding hm_record and its callers, so the later ruling does not lift the earlier one. Against the MODE 1 tests: porting with the callers is not impossible; nothing in the GM's words implies the split; the literal rule does not defeat the request's purpose. That edit-route and fragments may write neither file is a plausible argument about the clause's purpose, but it is the session completing a ruling's thought, and the block neither makes nor measures it. The caller list has no search behind it, and item 9's done-check greps only Makefile, *.mk and *.sh, so it cannot see a Python import of hm_record or a guard's by-path run; FR-003's 'no piece runs both' is therefore unshown. To clear: port the callers and the three guards in the cut, or have the round arbiter rule through make arbiter-ask that hm_record's read-only verbs may land ahead of them, with a caller census that names its search space.

decisions.summary: Python callers of hm_house.py and moves.py reach the ports through scripts/record_door.py, one process a run.
decisions.why: Adjudicated apart from hm_record: FR-001's one-cut clause does not name hm_house.py or moves.py; hm_house.py is placed in phase 3 with no such condition. A door to a ported piece has precedent in the spec (plan_door.py, preflight's door) and one process a run is in FR-006's direction.

Within only while nothing runs them (FR-003), which the hm_record-door decision's missing census leaves unshown. T84 is not in the bundle. FR-001's rewrite of recorded measurements that run a ported file falls in the commit that ports it, whatever the deletion date.

decisions.summary: Each port is proved by a differential on the real tree, Python against verb on exit, stdout and stderr; americanize's evidence is the paragraph run, the whole-file run having compared nothing; Rust's \s is fixed to match Python on U+001C-U+001F.

The killed whole-file run is disclosed and claimed as nothing. The bundle cannot show whether a kept test or suite case holds a whole-file input; if one does, FR-002 binds that case, and the Python is still present to compare against. The \s fix brings the port to the Python's output, which FR-002 requires.

decisions.why: Sequencing and exits inside FR-001 to FR-003; no researched value moves.

decisions.summary: scripts/checks_door.py is one process a run, but is reopened if the environment it reads changes mid-run, because land.py exports SPECIFY_FEATURE.
decisions.why: The ruling says a run's verbs go through one door process (FR-006), and this is a case where the run has more than one. A running process cannot see a variable its parent exported after it started, while the Python it replaces read the changed value in-process, so holding literally to one process would give different answers and defeat FR-002 and the door's own 'no logic' terms. FR-006's purpose, the import graph kept per process and not rebuilt per call, is untouched: the reopen happens only when the environment changes, and the differential carries 6 such cases.

decisions.why: The ruling moves every Python caller to the door, so the verbs those callers need follow from it; adding verbs narrows nothing. keep_batches is the outside-writer clause.

The end state does not move. The stated blind spot of the ast closure (a by-path run outside the import graph) is covered by the writers census, whose name search is over every *.py regardless of import graph.

decisions.summary: Where the Python's stderr holds a traceback only the traceback itself is unbound: what either side wrote before the Traceback line is compared, with exit status and stdout; one case of the 9,455 reached it, with no text before its traceback.
decisions.why: CHANGED since the BLOCKED reading. The earlier text set aside both sides' whole stderr, which reached a tool's own words printed before a traceback, words ask:449-usage-text keeps bound. The new text unbinds only the traceback's text and holds exit status and stdout, which is exactly the ruled case in FR-002, and it measures how many cases reached it.

decisions.summary: In the 102-invocation behavior comparison on the pre-split fixture clone, one verdict differs. check research-pointers' fixture list now names the crate paths, so on the pre-split tree it reads the moved files' fixtures as unexempted. The exits call this 'the ruled path difference'.
decisions.why: The plan's 'ruled' label is wrong, so this ruling is mine. ask:449-T92-messages covers only a path in a message the Rust itself writes, and it binds every other verdict byte for byte. A fixture or exemption list is data the check reads, and what differs here is a verdict, so the ask does not reach it. It is still legitimate on physical grounds. The split the GM asked for moves the files. A check that finds fixtures by path cannot exempt them at a path that no longer exists. Keeping the old list would make the check refuse correct work on the split tree, which is the case FR-002 itself carves out (constitution XIV). The difference shows up only when the new binary runs on the old tree. On the tree each binary is built for, the verdict is unchanged. The exits line should say 'the path difference ruled in this plan review', not cite the ask.

Dropping the forced build is the very behavior SC-006 removes, not a narrowing of test coverage; a changed guard crate still gets its one real build.

decisions.summary: The case's last check no longer pipes from sleep 30 (which the suite waited on every run) and judges in the suite's own shell, so its ok/bad reaches the counts (30 cases became 31).

decisions.summary: The Rust checks' runner becomes its own crate rust/gate/crates/rustc (over core and tree only) with its own binary l7r-rust, built and run by l7r-gate.sh rust <cmd>, stale only over core, tree, rustc, rust/guard and the workspace manifests; the wrapper's staleness scan gains rust/guard and touches the binary after a build.
decisions.why: The before-figures (labeled, observed 2026-11-11) attribute 40 s of a core edit's 49 s to the wrapper rebuilding the full release binary before any test ran. Splitting the runner off is the GM's 'splitting the gate crate into several crates' and FR-011's 'an edit recompiles one crate and what depends on it'; adding rust/guard to the staleness scan fixes a stale-binary hole. Nothing asked is narrowed.

decisions.summary: A crate's test, cover, lint and dead rerun only when its key moves: its sources, path dependencies (followed against every crate), workspace manifests, and the tree paths its tests read at run time as declared in [package.metadata.l7r] reads; a crate whose sources name the tree and declare nothing is refused with the fix named.
decisions.why: This is the GM's 'reuse ... the results of tests which have already run' and FR-011's reuse of a passed result. Keying on declared runtime reads makes a crate rerun when its tests' inputs change, which keeps a reused green truthful rather than narrowing reuse. The refusal of an undeclared reader is behavior, but its only reach is the soundness of the requested reuse: delete the reuse and it has nothing to check, so it enforces the request. (The incidental '1,105 lines' in this bullet carries no observation label; it narrates why a file was split and no decision rests on it.)

decisions.summary: When the first key moved, test and test-counters consult a second key: the crate's compiled test binaries plus every non-source input; a binary that already passed runs nothing, and the counting build shares the plain build's verdict where the binary is byte-identical (every crate but core and phases, observed 2026-11-11).
decisions.why: This is FR-011's literal 'run only the crates whose compiled test binary changed since their last green run'.

decisions.summary: Content ids are git blob ids whether a file is edited, staged or committed, and the last eight green keys are kept.
decisions.why: Implementation detail of the reuse so a commit, or an edit taken back, does not re-run what already passed; serves the request's reuse and narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: The only ways to run every crate fresh: FRESH=1 REASON="..." on make rust-test, make static or make counters-inert (refused without a two-word reason, logged through LOGESCAPE/guard_log), or make done FULL=1, which sets L7R_RUST_FRESH and runs bypass-audit first (asks for a reason at a terminal, cancels on empty, refuses with no terminal or from a backgrounded call, records the reason or the refusal via l7r-gate log bypass). FULL on the three targets and INCREMENTAL=0 anywhere no longer turn reuse off; the idle run's make done INCREMENTAL=0 keeps reuse for the Rust checks; no new guard.
decisions.why: FR-011: 'every crate at once only through an escape that states a reason and is recorded', and the GM's 'our tooling must enforce this'. Both named escapes now state a reason and are recorded (the previous round's text left make done FULL=1 as 'its own logged path' without saying it states a reason; the block now spells that out), and the block names no third unlogged route. Retiring FULL and INCREMENTAL=0 as reuse switches closes unrecorded escapes, which is enforcement of the request. The idle run keeping reuse extends reuse to a path the request does not mention rather than narrowing anything asked ('reuse ... results of tests which have already run ... is exactly what we should be doing'). Enforcement by making the slow run unreachable without a recorded reason satisfies FR-011's stated mechanism, so 'no new guard' narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: The l7r-gate rust verbs answer byte for byte as before except the kept-result line (now also for test, a named crate and a second-key hit) and the new undeclared-reader refusal.
decisions.why: The only output changes are the reuse report and the refusal, both parts of the requested reuse. FR-002 binds ports and T93 is not one, so its citation is loose, but that is not a fidelity finding.

decisions.summary: T93 is not a straight port under FR-001c and keeps its review; ordered after T92 and T94; exits and done-measures are the after-figures, make static, make hooks-test HOOKS_ALL=1, make done green, and FRESH=1 refused without a reason and logged with one; FR-004 coverage holds for the new crate.
decisions.why: Keeping the review applies FR-001c correctly (no Python is replaced). The order and exits follow FR-011's T92-T94 and SC-006's re-measurement. The FR-003 to FR-004 citation fix corrects the coverage constraint to the requirement that carries it.

decisions.summary: The gate binary builds in a new [profile.tool] (inherits release, incremental on) instead of release; [profile.release] left at cargo's default so the hamlet engine's cargo run --release is untouched.
decisions.why: This is the means of cutting the exact cost FR-012 names for T95 (the full l7r-gate release binary rebuilt after any gate crate edit). Leaving release alone keeps the engine's build and output unchanged, which SC-007 and the plan's no-map-moved answer require.

decisions.id: T95-D2 guard and l7r-rust share the profile
decisions.summary: l7r-guard and l7r-rust move to the tool profile with l7r-gate; the guard wrapper, its self-check and kept copy read tool/l7r-guard.
decisions.why: This reaches past the one binary FR-012 names for T95. It is still inside the GM's 'performance efficiency of the Rust code that we already have' (the Rust tooling's own costs), and the wrappers share one build. The block measured that it holds outputs: identical stdout and exit codes on four hook inputs, median and p90 latency no worse. It changes how the guard is built, not what it decides.

decisions.summary: test-l7r-guard.sh's fake cargo refuses a build without --profile tool; one case each in test-make-only-hooks.sh and make_only_hooks/tests.rs pins a tool/l7r-gate path; make_only_hooks code unchanged (matches by name).
decisions.why: These tests fail only if the wrapper drifts back to release or the make-only guard stops covering the moved binaries (FR-005). They enforce the requested change, so they are not added scope.

decisions.summary: codegen-units=256, opt-level 1, lto=off and the dev profile rejected on the bench.
decisions.why: These are design choices among ways to cut the same cost. The ones rejected for slowing the verbs were rejected to keep FR-012's 'held to every output and verdict' and no-slower runs.

decisions.summary: The rust-lld linker (about 0.4 s more) is left out of this landing.
decisions.why: FR-012 asks that the cost be cut and measured lower (SC-007), not cut as far as it can go. The cost falls from tens of seconds to about 2 s without it, so leaving out a further optimization narrows nothing that was asked.

decisions.summary: The hamlet engine's run and bench.rs's baseline build (an older commit whose manifest may not define the profile) stay on release; l7r-guard bench compares verdicts, not times.
decisions.why: Neither is the T95 cost. Keeping the engine on release protects generator output. The bench baseline builds an old manifest and compares verdicts only, so its profile does not touch anything FR-012 asks for.

decisions.summary: T95 goes first of T95-T99 because T96 touches the same profile settings.
decisions.why: The GM approved the five options together and gave no order, so sequencing them is inside the request.

decisions.id: T95-D8 make static remainder left to T96
decisions.summary: After an edit, make static still takes 103 s (core) or 65 s (claims). About 2 s of that is the gate rebuild; the rest (lint, coverage and dead-code reruns from T93's key) is left as T96's measurement.
decisions.why: T95's FR-012 cost is the gate binary rebuild only, and that is what T95 cuts. The remainder is not T95's to cut. Aside for the GM: T96's FR-012 remit is 'a test binary rebuilt after a one-line edit', and the lint and dead-code part of the remainder is not named in any of T95-T99. That belongs to the GM's 'stop and measure again' step, not to a T95 finding.

decisions.summary: The tool/ target is 485 MB against release's 141 MB, a cold tool build takes 34.1 s, and the first make rust-test after landing reruns every crate once (88 s).
decisions.why: FR-012 leaves a fresh worktree's cold build as it is, and the GM said 'I'm less concerned about the one-time ramp-up for a fresh clone'. Disk use and a one-time rerun are costs, not departures from what was asked.

decisions.summary: Exits: green on the guard suite, rust-test, static, identical verbs and land; red is set down and a cannot-be-done claim goes to make arbiter-ask. Budget is one landing. The generator perf tools are declared not applicable.
decisions.why: This is the procedure for carrying out the request. The generator tools do not apply because no engine code changes. Notes, which do not block: (1) the 'runs no slower and says the same' comparison names 8 verbs and gives no census of l7r-gate's verbs, so it may be a sample. SC-007's 'every check it touches' is also carried by the 19 crates of make rust-test, the 31-case guard suite, make static and make land, all green on the change. A later round may ask for the census. (2) The block's 'before' figures (core 38-45 s, owed 19-21 s, claims 8.0-8.6 s) differ from the figures the GM was shown ('claims 13.9 s, owed 8.4 s, core 10 s'), and the block does not explain the gap. FR-012's same-command rule is met because bench.py measured both sides, and the cost is lower against either baseline, but the GM may want the difference explained.

decisions.summary: The GM's 13.9 s for claims was a test rebuild after a core edit and its revert (rebuilt through core, tree, owed, plan); a claims-only one-line edit costs 3.8-3.9 s, split into compile and GNU ld link.
decisions.why: Answers the GM's own 'Tell me more about these numbers' and locates the cost FR-012 names (T96); it narrows nothing: the core-edit path is also measured after the change (make static after a core edit, links 27-61 s to 3.7-4.1 s).

decisions.summary: Every cargo build links with the toolchain's rust-lld via one repository-root .cargo/config.toml.
decisions.why: The means of cutting the cost FR-012 asks cut; outputs held (coverage reports identical, 19 crates green, guard suite 37/37, 8 l7r-gate verbs identical).

decisions.summary: The dev profile (inherited by test) keeps line tables only for debug info.
decisions.why: A means of cutting link time and output size; the plan records coverage reports unchanged, so FR-012's hold on outputs is kept.

decisions.summary: l7r-gate.sh, l7r-guard.sh and rustc.rs run cargo from the tree's root so every build (cover's show-env included) reads the same config; coverage build keeps lld.
decisions.why: Implementation needed for the change to apply uniformly and not split build flags; changes no verdict or output.

decisions.summary: The config names the 1.87.0 gcc-ld directory; a moved toolchain makes l7r-gate.sh refuse, l7r-guard.sh keep its last good binary, and a rust-test fail, each naming the fix.
decisions.why: The approach's own failure handling for the path it hard-codes, not a carve-out from the request: on the toolchain the tree is built with, no verdict or output changes; it turns what would be an obscure link failure into a named one. No reach beyond the builds T96 changes.

decisions.summary: .cargo/config.toml joins the kept-result key's workspace files and rustc's declared reads.
decisions.why: Keeps FR-011's result reuse correct under the new config file (a config change reruns every crate); serves the requested reuse rather than adding scope.

decisions.summary: Release and tool profiles do not inherit dev's debug setting; the hamlet engine's code generation is unchanged, its release build relinks once with lld.
decisions.why: Confines the change to the tooling build time FR-012 targets; no map or engine output moves.

decisions.summary: opt-level 0 (option c) rejected as buying less; instrumenting only our crates for coverage (option e), the '.' reads and the dead-code key left to T100.
decisions.why: Choice among means for T96's cost; the deferred items are make static's coverage and dead-code reruns, which the GM filed as T100 and FR-012 assigns there, so nothing asked is dropped.

decisions.summary: After figures by the same make rust-test command (3.8 s to about 1 s for a claims edit) and make static after core and claims edits (103.3 to ~75 s, 64.8 to ~56 s), outputs re-verified.
decisions.why: SC-007's re-measure by the same command and verdict hold; every figure carries a one-shot observed/method label.

decisions.summary: A new guard, scratch-sweep-hooks, starts at most one detached sweep a day from UserPromptSubmit; make scratch-sweep [DRY=1] runs one on demand.
decisions.why: The GM: 'Fix those leaks as well' of the session scratch under /tmp/claude-1000; FR-013 asks for a sweep of finished sessions' scratch. A recurring sweep, with make as the one entry point (FR-005), is how the leak is fixed and nothing beyond it.

decisions.summary: A session directory goes when its transcript AND everything inside it have been unchanged three days; a session directory with no transcript and a loose top-level entry go when nothing inside changed in three days.
decisions.why: FR-013: swept 'once its transcript has been idle for days, never a live session's'. Also reading the directory's own contents is how 'never a live session's' is kept when a subagent writes there without touching the session's transcript, so it carries the spec's own constraint. Directories with no transcript and loose entries are scratch under /tmp/claude-1000 too, part of the 38 GB leak the GM said to fix, and are judged by the same idle rule.

decisions.summary: Three days idle, swept once a day, as GUESS knobs (SCRATCH_SWEEP_DAYS) with seams for the tests.
decisions.why: FR-013 says 'idle for days' and gives no number. Three days fills that in and also meets the relay's 'don't touch dirs younger than a few hours'.

decisions.summary: Always kept: the prompting session's directory, every session registered as running in ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json whose pid still runs and whose procStart matches, and any entry a live process holds as its cwd, binary or open file.
decisions.why: This is FR-013's 'never a live session's' itself. A session paused over a weekend has an idle transcript but is still live, so the registry and /proc checks are what make that clause hold.

decisions.summary: Where the session registry cannot be read, no session directory is judged at all.
decisions.why: Without the registry the sweep cannot tell a live session paused past three days from a finished one. Sweeping anyway would break FR-013's 'never a live session's', which is the GM's own constraint, so the exception is implied by the request's own words. It covers session directories only, and loose entries are still swept. Checked 2026-11-11 with ls -la ~/.claude/sessions/ on this container: the registry is present and readable by uid 1000, and its records carry pid and procStart. So the fail-safe is not the default on the machine that has the leak.

decisions.summary: Nothing is removed where /proc cannot be read.
decisions.why: Without /proc the sweep cannot see which entries live processes hold, so removing would risk exactly what FR-013 forbids. The exception is implied by 'never a live session's'. On this Linux container /proc is readable, so the case is a fail-safe and does not hollow out the sweep.

decisions.summary: Any tree containing a directory the sweep cannot read is kept.
decisions.why: The sweep cannot establish that nothing inside changed in three days, or that no live process holds it, without reading the tree. Removing it would need the idle test that FR-013 sets as the condition for sweeping, and that test cannot be run here, so the rule cannot be applied as written. The case is per-tree and does not exempt the readable scratch the leak is made of.

decisions.summary: Links are never followed or descended: a link inside a removed tree is deleted as itself with its target untouched, and a link at the root or among a project's sessions is left.
decisions.why: The scope is scratch UNDER /tmp/claude-1000, and following a link could delete or judge something outside it. A link at the root or in a session slot holds no disk itself, and its idleness and liveness could only be judged by following it out of the root, which the request's scope forbids. Leaving it frees nothing less, so the leak fix's purpose is untouched. Links inside a removed tree are still removed, so no scratch survives through them.

decisions.summary: The hook reads only the stamp's age and starts the sweep with setsid -f; the sweep takes a lock, rechecks the stamp and writes it before walking. Cost recorded with labeled figures.
decisions.why: This is how the sweep runs (cost and concurrency) and settles nothing about what is or is not swept. All figures carry observed-date and method labels.

decisions.summary: Every removal and the day's total are written to the guard log with sizes.
decisions.why: It makes the requested sweep checkable and adds no behavior.

decisions.summary: A dry run on this machine would remove 110 entries, 11.0 MB; the large trees were already cleared by the laptop session.
decisions.why: This is a labeled measurement. It does not conflict with FR-013's 'the existing pile is left to the GM's laptop session': the plan does not do a separate cleanup of the pile, the laptop session has already cleared the large trees, and the forward sweep that FR-013 asks for applies its idle rule to whatever is there.

decisions.summary: A project directory left empty is kept.
decisions.why: A project directory is a container for many sessions, not a finished session's scratch, which is the subject of FR-013 and SC-008. Empty, it holds no meaningful disk.

decisions.summary: Checklist part A: goal, constraints, order after T96 beside T101 (T102 extends to the cargo cache), exits through make land and arbiter-ask, and a done measure (504 tests passed, the dry run).
decisions.why: It restates FR-013 and records process, and narrows nothing. Its figures are labeled.

decisions.summary: Every TempDir::new removes each l7r-{tag}-p{pid}-{seq} directory of its tag in its parent whose pid has no /proc entry, and hookrun.sh removes l7r-hooks-suite-<guard>-p<pid>.* of a gone pid before each run; neither sweep has any age condition.
decisions.why: Arbiter check 1: yes, the liveness test can remove a directory a live process still holds. The pid in the name is the CREATOR's, but the holders are mostly its descendants: under make rust-test the runner's TempDir is the TMPDIR of cargo and every test binary, and hookrun.sh's suite directory is held by the suite it runs. Kill the creator alone (SIGKILL, or a TERM aimed at its pid by a watchdog or timeout rather than at its group, which by the paragraph's own premise the Rust runner does not handle) and the children live on; the next run of the same tag or guard finds no /proc entry and deletes the directory under them. The plan calls pid reuse 'the safe way to be wrong' and never names this unsafe way. The request names exactly this risk and the rule against it: 'don't touch dirs younger than a few hours (a running gate may own them)'. The sweep deletes directories of any age, and the plan never mentions that clause. Substituting a pid test for the GM's age floor because it looks more precise is not a ground under MODE 1: an age floor is not impossible, nothing else the GM wrote contradicts it, and it does not defeat the purpose (the pile stays bounded). What the plan must carry: the GM's floor, so that neither sweep touches a directory younger than a few hours, whatever its pid.

decisions.summary: TempDir names directories l7r-{tag}-p{pid}-{seq} and sweeps only that form, so the pre-T101 l7r-{tag}-{pid}-{seq} pile (and mktemp-suffixed names) is never touched and stays the laptop session's to delete.
decisions.why: Arbiter check 2: yes, as long as the match is anchored. An exact tag, then '-p', digits, '-', digits, then end of name cannot match the old l7r-{tag}-{pid}-{seq} form (no 'p') or a mktemp XXXXXX suffix (no hyphen inside it). The bundle shows the NAME FORM, not the matcher, so this ruling assumes an anchored match. The unit test's old-form and other-tag fixtures pin that on the Rust side, and test-parts.sh's old-form fixture pins it on the shell side. Leaving the pile alone follows the request's 'leave that alone unless he asks you to' and FR-013's last sentence.

decisions.summary: A pid reused by a live process keeps the directory carrying that pid.
decisions.why: Arbiter check 3: yes, by construction. A /proc/<pid> entry that is present, a zombie's included, means the directory is kept, and the unit test's live-pid fixture and test-parts.sh's live-run fixture go through that same branch. The only cost is a leftover lasting until the pid is freed and a later run of that tag, which errs in the direction the request asks for.

decisions.summary: hookrun.sh stops the suite and exits through its EXIT trap on INT or TERM, and sweeps gone-pid suite directories; a unit test sweeps a fixture of gone-pid, live-pid, other-tag and old-form directories; tests/hooks/test-parts.sh runs hookrun.sh beside a gone run's, a live run's and an old-form directory and stops one with TERM, two of its cases red against the earlier hookrun.sh.
decisions.why: Arbiter check 4: they match, with two gaps in what is pinned. They are recorded here and do not block. (a) test-parts.sh sends only TERM, so the INT half of hookrun.sh's trap, which the plan claims, is pinned by nothing. (b) The unit test has an 'another tag's' fixture but the shell pin has no other-guard fixture, so whether hookrun.sh's sweep is confined to its own <guard> goes unchecked. 'Two of its cases red against the earlier hookrun.sh' is consistent: only the gone-run removal and the TERM exit could fail against a version that neither sweeps nor traps, while the live and old-form cases pin against a sweep that reaches too far. These tests enforce the request ('add a test that pins it') and are in scope.

decisions.summary: Left line, SIGKILL part: a process killed by SIGKILL leaves its directory until the next of its kind runs.
decisions.why: The request says 'remove it on exit, including failure and interrupt', and FR-013 says 'removed on exit, failure and panic included'. No code runs in a process on SIGKILL, so removing the directory at that exit cannot be done at all. Removing it on a later run is the most that is possible, and under make rust-test the runner's per-run TMPDIR already holds every test's scratch for that run.

decisions.summary: Left line, INT/TERM part: the paragraph treats SIGINT and SIGTERM 'as surely as SIGKILL', so a Rust process (the make rust-test runner, a test binary, a production command) stopped by an interrupt or a TERM leaves its directory until the next of its kind runs instead of removing it on exit.
decisions.why: MODE 1's rule on bundled cases: one argument stretched over two unlike things. SIGKILL cannot be caught. SIGINT and SIGTERM can, and only their DEFAULT handling skips Drop. The plan itself traps INT and TERM in hookrun.sh and parts.sh, stopping the children and then removing the directory, which shows the Rust runner's counterpart is possible. The request names this case word for word: 'remove it on exit, including failure and interrupt (trap / ...)'. Under FR-013 ('removed on exit') an interrupted process has exited and its directory has not been removed. Being harder to do in Rust, or the sweep already bounding the pile, does not make the exception legitimate. What the plan must carry: on an interrupt or a TERM, the Rust side removes what it made at exit, as the shell side already does, so that the Left line keeps only SIGKILL.

decisions.summary: The cargo target cache is pruned by extending T103's daily sweep (same lock, stamp, live-process check, log and make scratch-sweep [DRY=1]).
decisions.why: FR-013 and the GM's 'Fix those leaks as well' ask that the cache stop growing without bound and leave the mechanism open. A periodic prune is a direct means to that end and narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: Within a store, each crate's variants beyond its newest four are removed once idle three days.
decisions.why: This bounds growth from moved paths and changed flags, which serves SC-008. One caveat: the premise that cargo makes a new variant only on a path or flag change is stated, not measured, and the bundle does not show how variants are grouped. Per-run-named crates (l7r_fixture_broken_<n>) would escape a per-name cap. What covers the measured leak is the dry run, which reports the l7r_fixture variants removed, and the fact that the source is gone. The cap's adequacy therefore rests on the dry run, not on the rule as written. That is a design caveat, not a narrowing: nothing the GM asked for is excluded.

decisions.summary: A build directory named for no live tree is removed whole after three idle days. The mirror's and every clone's directories are never removed whole. Where the clones directory cannot be read, nothing is removed whole.
decisions.why: Live trees' directories are still variant-pruned, so growth stays bounded. The protections keep the guard's binary and live builds safe, in line with the relayed caution not to touch what a running gate may own. Nothing asked for is narrowed.

decisions.summary: Anything a live process holds is kept, as in T103.
decisions.why: A safety condition in line with the relayed 'don't touch dirs ... a running gate may own'. It does not limit the leak fix.

decisions.summary: The sweep's first run removes stale content already in the cache: about 2.4 GB, including six stale build directories.
decisions.why: FR-013's 'the existing pile is left to the GM's laptop session' comes from the relayed message, where 'the existing pile' is defined in the preceding sentence as the /tmp l7r-* scratch directories (T101). The GM's only words on the cargo cache are 'Fix those leaks as well', and a sweep that fixes a growth leak necessarily removes what is stale. T103 did the same for /tmp/claude-1000 and was cleared. The three-day idle threshold and the live-process check go beyond the 'younger than a few hours' caution.

decisions.summary: Four variants and three idle days are new constants, labeled GUESS knobs.
decisions.why: These are parameters of the requested mechanism, declared as guesses and not claimed as measurements. They narrow nothing.

decisions.summary: 'Done, measured' is the dry run, with the mechanism pinned by fixture tests.
decisions.why: The dry run shows what the sweep removes today, not SC-008's property that the cache's size stops growing with test runs. The fixture tests cover the mechanism that gives that property. This is a plan-quality point and narrows nothing the GM asked for.
